name: Sara Martino #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: sara.martino@ntnu.no affiliations: Dept. of Mathematical Science, NTNU - name: Janine Illian #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: Janine.Illian@glasgow.ac.uk affiliations: University of Glasgow - name: Jafet Belmont #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: Jafet.Belmont@glasgow.ac.uk affiliations: University of Glasgow # date: May 22, 2025 # bibliography: references.bib embed-resources: true execute: echo: true allow-html: true freeze: auto editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- # The `inlabru` workflow ## The syntax {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"} ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1,2,3"} # Define model components comps <- component_1(...) + component_2(...) + ... # Define the model predictor pred <- linear_function(component_1, component_2, ...) # Build the observation model lik <- bru_obs(formula = pred, family = ... , data = ... , ...) # Fit the model fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Components** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ~ my_component_name( main = ..., model = ... ) ``` ::: - `my_component_name` how you label your component (.e.g, `beta_0`,`myspde`) - `main` input data for the component (e.g., a the name of a column in your data or a spatial object) - `model` The type of model component (e.g., `linear`,`fixed`,`iid`,`rw1`,`rw2`,`ar1`, see `?INLA::inla.list.models()$latent`) ::: ::::: ## The syntax {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"} ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="5,6,7"} # Define model components comps <- component_1(...) + component_2(...) + ... # Define the model predictor pred <- linear_function(component_1, component_2, ...) # Build the observation model lik <- bru_obs(formula = pred, family = ... , data = ... , ...) # Fit the model fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **linear predictor** - can be defined within the formula: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lik = bru_obs(formula = response ~ component_1(...) + component_2(...), family, data) ``` ::: - or use a full stop short-code after the components have been defined ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lik = bru_obs(formula = response ~., family, data) ``` ::: ::: ::::: ## The syntax {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"} ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="9,10,11,12,13|16,17"} # Define model components comps <- component_1(...) + component_2(...) + ... # Define the model predictor pred <- linear_function(component_1, component_2, ...) # Build the observation model lik <- bru_obs(formula = pred, family = ... , data = ... , ...) # Fit the model fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Likelihood** Specify the distribution family (see `inla.list.models("likelihood")`) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lik = bru_obs(formula, family = "gaussian", data = df) ``` ::: ::: ::::: ## Why do we need the -1 in the formula? {.smaller} - `inlabru` provides a dedicated term, `Intercept()`, for specifying an intercept that is shared across all data. - When this term is omitted, a common intercept is added by default, unless the formula or component explicitly includes `-1`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df = data.frame(covariate = runif(100)) df = df %>% mutate(y = 1 + 0.5 *covariate + rnorm(100)) ``` ::: :::::: columns ::: {.column width="33.33%"} **Wrong** :x: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp = ~ beta0(1) + beta1(covariate, model = "linear") lik = bru_obs(formula = y ~ . , data = df) m1 = bru(cmp, lik) round(m1$summary.fixed[,c(1,2)],3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean sd beta0 0.704 22.361 beta1 -0.046 0.337 Intercept 0.704 22.361 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33.33%"} **Correct** :white_check_mark: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp = ~ Intercept(1) + beta1(covariate, model = "linear") lik = bru_obs(y~ ., data = df) m1 = bru(cmp, lik) round(m1$summary.fixed[,c(1,2)],3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean sd Intercept 1.408 0.186 beta1 -0.045 0.337 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33.33%"} **Correct** :white_check_mark: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp = ~ -1 + beta0(1) + beta1(covariate, model = "linear") lik = bru_obs(y~. , data = df) m1 = bru(cmp, lik) round(m1$summary.fixed[,c(1,2)],3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean sd beta0 1.408 0.186 beta1 -0.045 0.337 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::::: # Categorical variables and interactions ## Categorical variables and Interactions `inlabru` has a specific component type for this that is called `fixed`. Let's look at the `iris` dataset that is in `R` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(iris) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species 1 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2 setosa 2 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2 setosa 3 4.7 3.2 1.3 0.2 setosa 4 4.6 3.1 1.5 0.2 setosa 5 5.0 3.6 1.4 0.2 setosa 6 5.4 3.9 1.7 0.4 setosa ``` ::: ::: ![](figures/setosa.jpg){fig-align="center"} ## Effects of categorical variables in `inlabru` {.smaller} We want to fit a model where `Species` is the only covariate. - `Species` has three categories: `setosa`, `versicolor` and `virginica` - We want to model it as a factor effect $$\begin{aligned} y_i & \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma_y), \\ \mu_i &= \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{0,\text{versicolor}}\, x_{i2} + \beta_{0,\text{virginica}}\, x_{i3} \end{aligned}$$ $x_{ij} = 1$ if flower $i$ belongs to species $j$ (1 = Setosa, 2 = Versicolor, 3 = Virginica) and 0 otherwise. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} iris$Species = factor(iris$Species) m1 = lm(Sepal.Length ~ Species, data = iris) m1$coef ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) Speciesversicolor Speciesvirginica 5.006 0.930 1.582 ``` ::: ::: Here *I. setosa* is our reference category! ::: fragment How do we do this in `inlabru`? ::: ## Effects of categorical variables in `inlabru`{.smaller} **Parametrization 1**: Reference category. Use the `fixed` model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp1 = ~ -1 + spp(~ Species, model = "fixed") lik1 = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~., data = iris) fit1 = bru(cmp1, lik1) fit1$summary.random$spp[,c(1:3)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID mean sd 1 (Intercept) 5.0059868 0.07268942 2 Speciesversicolor 0.9300083 0.10279837 3 Speciesvirginica 1.5820048 0.10279837 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: callout-note - `spp(~ Species, model = "fixed")` is a `lm` style model definition! So an intercept is automatically included - The results are stored in the `summary.random` part of the model, not the `summary.fixed` ::: ## Effects of categorical variables in `inlabru`{.smaller} **Parametrization 2**: No reference category ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1"} cmp2 = ~ -1 + spp(~ -1 + Species, model = "fixed") lik2 = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~., data = iris) fit2 = bru(cmp2, lik2) fit2$summary.random$spp[,c(1:3)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID mean sd 1 Speciessetosa 5.005974 0.07268959 2 Speciesversicolor 5.935969 0.07268959 3 Speciesvirginica 6.587965 0.07268959 ``` ::: ::: . . . This is just a re-parametrization from our previous model :::::: columns ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coef = fit1$summary.random$spp c( coef[1,2], coef[1,2] + coef[2,2], coef[1,2] + coef[3,2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5.005987 5.935995 6.587992 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"} - $\beta_0$: mean sepal length for *I. setosa* - $\beta_0 + \beta_{0,\text{versicolor}}$ : mean sepal length for for *I. versicolor* - $\beta_0 + \beta_{0,\text{virginica}}$: mean sepal length for for *I. virginica* ::: :::: :::::: ## Interactions of linear covariates in `inlabru`{.smaller} Here the easiest option is to use again the `fixed` model type. . . . Say we want to fit a model with interactions between (**categorical**) `Species` and and (**continuous**) `Petal.Length`. ::: panel-tabset ## `lm` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m2 = lm(Sepal.Length ~ Species * Petal.Length, data = iris) m2$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) Speciesversicolor 4.2131682 -1.8056451 Speciesvirginica Petal.Length -3.1535091 0.5422926 Speciesversicolor:Petal.Length Speciesvirginica:Petal.Length 0.2859884 0.4534460 ``` ::: ::: ## `inlabru` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp = ~ -1 + fixed_effects( ~ ( Species * Petal.Length), model = "fixed") lik = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~ ., data = iris) fit = bru(cmp, lik) fit$summary.random$fixed_effects$mean ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.2116296 -1.8037483 -3.1512099 0.5433309 0.2848670 0.4522720 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fit$summary.random$fixed_effects$sd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.4066569 0.5973285 0.6329055 0.2762482 0.2944992 0.2895899 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Getting results from the fitted model ## The `result` object {.smaller} The fitted model is stored in an `inlabru` object Let's ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ask inlabru to compute DIC adn WAIC bru_options_set(control.compute = list(dic = T, waic = T)) cmp = ~ -1 + spp( ~ Species, model = "fixed") + petal_length(Petal.Length, model = "linear") + petal_width(Petal.Width, model = "linear") lik = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~ ., data = iris ) result = bru(cmp, lik) summary(result) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` inlabru version: 2.15.0 INLA version: 26.08.22 Latent components: spp: main = fixed(~Species) petal_length: main = linear(Petal.Length) petal_width: main = linear(Petal.Width) Observation models: Model tag: Family: 'gaussian' Data class: 'data.frame' Response class: 'numeric' Predictor: Sepal.Length ~ spp + petal_length + petal_width Additive/Linear/Rowwise: TRUE/TRUE/TRUE Used components: effect[spp, petal_length, petal_width], latent[] Time used: Pre = 0.36, Running = 0.697, Post = 0.0927, Total = 1.15 Fixed effects: mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld petal_length 0.906 0.074 0.760 0.906 1.052 0.906 0 petal_width -0.006 0.156 -0.312 -0.006 0.300 -0.006 0 Random effects: Name Model spp IID model Model hyperparameters: mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant Precision for the Gaussian observations 8.81 1.03 6.92 8.77 0.975quant mode Precision for the Gaussian observations 10.94 8.69 Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) ...............: 108.27 Deviance Information Criterion (DIC, saturated) ....: 158.51 Effective number of parameters .....................: 6.01 Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 108.56 Effective number of parameters .................: 6.02 Marginal log-Likelihood: -88.11 is computed Posterior summaries for the linear predictor and the fitted values are computed (Posterior marginals needs also 'control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)') ``` ::: ::: ## Getting results I {.smaller} Some results are very easy to get as they are contained in the `result` object: - Summaries for fixed effects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} result$summary.fixed ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant petal_length 0.90592400 0.07418197 0.7602547 0.905924148 1.051592 petal_width -0.00605831 0.15598983 -0.3123721 -0.006057885 0.300253 mode kld petal_length 0.905924147 3.803196e-09 petal_width -0.006057889 3.803470e-09 ``` ::: ::: . . . - Summaries for random effects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} result$summary.random$spp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ID mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant 1 (Intercept) 3.683013 0.1072158 3.472477 3.683012 3.893550 2 Speciesversicolor -1.598212 0.2053419 -2.001432 -1.598213 -1.194985 3 Speciesvirginica -2.112424 0.3034847 -2.708363 -2.112425 -1.516476 mode kld 1 3.683012 3.803059e-09 2 -1.598213 3.802046e-09 3 -2.112425 3.801948e-09 ``` ::: ::: . . . - Summaries for hyperparameters ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} result$summary.hyperpar ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant Precision for the Gaussian observations 8.811673 1.027757 6.914679 8.771938 0.975quant mode Precision for the Gaussian observations 10.93846 8.692115 ``` ::: ::: ## Getting results I {.smaller} - Marginals for fixed effects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} result$marginals.fixed$petal_width[1:3,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x y [1,] -0.6873659 0.0002767216 [2,] -0.5971039 0.0023763658 [3,] -0.4937156 0.0206614483 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} result$marginals.fixed$petal_length[1:3,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x y [1,] 0.5819249 0.0005818918 [2,] 0.6248493 0.0049970578 [3,] 0.6740160 0.0434471438 ``` ::: ::: . . . - Summaries for random effects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} result$marginals.random$spp$index.1[1:3,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x y [1,] 3.214741 0.0004026112 [2,] 3.276779 0.0034575330 [3,] 3.347838 0.0300615540 ``` ::: ::: . . . - Summaries for hyperparameters ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} result$marginals.hyperpar$`Precision for the Gaussian observations`[1:3,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x y [1,] 5.530671 0.0006337919 [2,] 5.642802 0.0010993444 [3,] 5.995599 0.0047247741 ``` ::: ::: ## `predict()` and `generate()` functions {.smaller} Often one wants more "complex" results from the model. Suppose we fit a model with the following linear predictor $$\eta_i = \beta_{0,\text{Species}_i} + \beta_{1,\text{Species}_i}\text{Petal Length}_i,\ i =1,\dots,n$$ We might want to recover the three regression lines - $\eta_i = \beta_{0,\text{Setosa}} + \beta_{1,\text{Setosa}}\text{Petal Length}_i$ - $\eta_i = \beta_{0,\text{Virginica}} + \beta_{1,\text{Virginica}}\text{Petal Length}_i$ - $\eta_i = \beta_{0,\text{Versicolor}} + \beta_{1,\text{Versicolor}}\text{Petal Length}_i$ . . . To do this we can use the `predict()` and `generate()` functions. - `predict()` *simulates* from the fitted posterior distribution $\pi(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{u},\theta)$, computes what you ask and produces a summary of the samples (mean, sd, quantiles, etc) - `generate()` *simulates* from the fitted posterior distribution $\pi(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{u},\theta)$, computes what you ask and return the samples! ## Example 1 - predictions for the mean ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp = ~ -1 + fixed_effects(~Species * Petal.Length, model = "fixed") lik = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~ ., data = iris) fit = bru(cmp, lik) pred_grid <- iris %>% group_by(Species) %>% reframe(Petal.Length = seq(min(Petal.Length), max(Petal.Length), by = 0.1)) res = predict(fit, pred_grid, ~ fixed_effects) res[1:5,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Species Petal.Length mean sd q0.025 q0.5 q0.975 median 1 setosa 1.0 4.753904 0.14172201 4.476773 4.754597 5.076221 4.754597 2 setosa 1.1 4.808562 0.11455619 4.589169 4.808532 5.062371 4.808532 3 setosa 1.2 4.863221 0.08879795 4.700381 4.861741 5.048521 4.861741 4 setosa 1.3 4.917879 0.06611353 4.804205 4.919636 5.043803 4.919636 5 setosa 1.4 4.972538 0.05080243 4.881977 4.975566 5.066894 4.975566 mean.mc_std_err sd.mc_std_err 1 0.016272222 0.010500107 2 0.013159233 0.008518070 3 0.010190507 0.006553557 4 0.007544710 0.004666785 5 0.005731148 0.003254526 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 1 - predictions for the mean Notice that we predict only within the range of the covariate for each species: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res %>% ggplot() + geom_line(aes(Petal.Length, mean, group = Species, color = Species)) + geom_ribbon(aes(Petal.Length, ymin = q0.025 , ymax = q0.975, group = Species, fill = Species), alpha = 0.5)+ facet_wrap(~Species,scales="free_x") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](slides_2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Example 1 - predictions for new observations The uncertainty we have computed now is relative to the prediction of $\eta$. - If we want to predict a new observation, we need to add the observation (likelihood) uncertainty $\sigma^2_y$ - We compute a prediction interval using `generate()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} q_samples = generate(fit, pred_grid, formula = ~ { eta = fixed_effects sigma = sqrt(1/Precision_for_the_Gaussian_observations) c(qnorm(0.025, eta, sigma), qnorm(0.975, eta, sigma)) }, n.samples = 1000) pred_int = cbind(pred_grid, matrix(rowMeans(q_samples), ncol = 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("lower", "upper")))) ``` ::: ## Example 1 - predictions for new observations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot() + geom_point(data = iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Sepal.Length,color = Species)) + geom_line(data=res, aes(Petal.Length, mean, group = Species, color = Species))+ geom_ribbon(data=res,aes(Petal.Length, ymin = q0.025 , ymax = q0.975, group = Species, fill = Species), alpha = 0.5)+ geom_line(data = pred_int,aes(Petal.Length, lower), color = "red",lty=2) + geom_line(data = pred_int,aes(Petal.Length, upper), color = "red",lty=2) + facet_wrap(~Species,scales="free_x") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](slides_2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Example 2 {.smaller} We will look at the effect that incubation temperature has on the sex determination of turtles. Lets say we are interested in the number male turtles out of the total number of turtles that hatched. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data(turtle, package = "faraway") turtle$total <- turtle$male + turtle$female turtle$temp_c <- turtle$temp - mean(turtle$temp) glimpse(turtle) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 15 Columns: 5 $ temp 27.2, 27.2, 27.2, 27.7, 27.7, 27.7, 28.3, 28.3, 28.3, 28.4, 28.… $ male 1, 0, 1, 7, 4, 6, 13, 6, 7, 7, 5, 7, 10, 8, 9 $ female 9, 8, 8, 3, 2, 2, 0, 3, 1, 3, 3, 2, 1, 0, 0 $ total 10, 8, 9, 10, 6, 8, 13, 9, 8, 10, 8, 9, 11, 8, 9 $ temp_c -1.1, -1.1, -1.1, -0.6, -0.6, -0.6, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.1, 0.1, 0.… ``` ::: ::: ![](figures/turtles.jpg){fig-align="center"} ## Example 2 {.smaller} We begin fitting a logistic regression of the form: $$\begin{aligned} y_i \mid \eta_i &\sim \text{Binomial}(n_i, p_i)\\ \eta_i &= \text{logit}(p_i) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{temperature}_i \end{aligned}$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers=""} cmp = ~ -1 + beta_0(1) + beta_1(temp, model = "linear") lik = bru_obs(formula = male ~ beta_0 + beta_1, data = turtle, family = "binomial", Ntrials = turtle$total) fit_turtles = bru(cmp, lik) ``` ::: We now want to extract results...what do we want? . . . - The temperature effect $\beta_1 \text{temperature}_i$ ? - The linear predictor $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{temperature}_i$? - The estimated probability off a male being hatched $p_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i)$ ? We can get all of them with the `predict()` or `generate()` functions! ## Example - `predict()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} turtle_pred <- data.frame(temp = seq(27,30,0.1)) preds1 = predict(object = fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred, ~ beta_1) preds2 = predict(object = fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred, ~ beta_0 + beta_1) inv_logit = function(x) ((1 + exp(-x))^(-1)) preds3 = predict(object = fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred, ~ inv_logit(beta_0 + beta_1)) ``` ::: or ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} preds = predict( fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred, ~ data.frame(temp_eff = beta_1, lin_pred = beta_0 + beta_1, probs = inv_logit(beta_0 + beta_1)), n.samples = 1000 ) round(preds$probs[1:3,],3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` temp mean sd q0.025 q0.5 q0.975 median mean.mc_std_err sd.mc_std_err 1 27.0 0.199 0.065 0.096 0.190 0.346 0.190 0.002 0.002 2 27.1 0.231 0.067 0.121 0.224 0.375 0.224 0.002 0.002 3 27.2 0.267 0.068 0.152 0.261 0.410 0.261 0.002 0.002 ``` ::: ::: ## Example - `predict()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} preds$probs %>% ggplot() + geom_line(aes(temp, mean)) + geom_ribbon(aes(temp, ymin = q0.025, ymax = q0.975), alpha = 0.5)+ labs(y="p",x= "Temperature") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](slides_2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Example - `generate()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} samples = generate(fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred, ~ data.frame(temp_eff = beta_1, lin_pred = beta_0 + beta_1, probs = inv_logit(beta_0 + beta_1)), n.samples = 20) # samples is now a list of length 20 (n.samples) each element of the list looks like: samples[[1]][1:3,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` temp_eff lin_pred probs 1 65.13997 -1.802936 0.1414940 2 65.38123 -1.561677 0.1734061 3 65.62248 -1.320418 0.2107488 ``` ::: ::: ## Example - `generate()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame(temp = turtle_pred$temp, sapply(samples, function(x) x$probs)) %>% pivot_longer(-temp) %>% ggplot() + geom_line(aes(temp, value, group = name, color = factor(name))) + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](slides_2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Manipulating posterior marginals ## Manipulating posterior marginals We can be interested in functions of the posterior marginals that are computed by the `bru()` function. For example, we might want to : - compute the mean of a posterior marginal - compute the median of a posterior marginal - sample from the posterior marginal - ... All this can be done with the help of the `inla.*marginal()` family of functions ## Example from the iris data {auto-animate=TRUE} ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.7em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1"} post_prec = fit$marginals.hyperpar$`Precision for the Gaussian observations` # <1> post_sd = inla.tmarginal(fun = function(x) 1/sqrt(x), post_prec) post_sd_mode = inla.mmarginal(post_sd) post_sd_mean = inla.emarginal(fun =function(x)x, post_sd ) post_sd_sample = inla.rmarginal(1000, post_sd) ``` :::
1. ::: {style="font-size:0.5em;"} | **Function Name** | **Usage** | |---------------------------------------------|---------------------------| | `inla.dmarginal(x, marginal, ...)` | Density at a vector of evaluation points $x$ | | `inla.pmarginal(q, marginal, ...)` | Distribution function at a vector of quantiles *q* | | `inla.qmarginal(p, marginal, ...)` | Quantile function at a vector of probabilities *p* | | `inla.rmarginal(n, marginal)` | Generate *n* random deviates | | `inla.hpdmarginal(p, marginal, ...)` | Compute the highest posterior density interval at level *p* | | `inla.emarginal(fun, marginal, ...)` | Compute the expected value assuming transformation given by *fun* | | `inla.mmarginal(marginal)` | Computes the mode | | `inla.smarginal(marginal, ...)` | Smoothed density (returns x-values and interpolated y-values) | | `inla.tmarginal(fun, marginal, ...)` | Transform the marginal using function *fun* | | `inla.zmarginal(marginal)` | Summary statistics for the marginal | ::: # Getting help while using `inlabru` ## Which priors have I used?

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
